blogs.title: Encapsulation: Hiding Complexity, Exposing Intent
blogs.author: Sarfaraj Khatri
blogs.description:
Encapsulation is one of the foundational pillars of object-oriented programming, and yet it is often misunderstood or applied inconsistently across codebases. At its core, encapsulation is the practice of bundling data with the operations that manipulate that data and restricting direct access to some of an object's components. This article explores encapsulation from first principles and demonstrates how a disciplined approach pays dividends in maintainability, testability, and reasoning about systems.

We begin by defining encapsulation in practical terms: using access modifiers (public, protected, private) to enforce boundaries, preferring immutable objects where appropriate, and exposing behavior through small, intention-revealing methods rather than public mutable fields. The article contains concrete examples in C# and TypeScript that show how readonly fields, private setters, and defensive copying prevent subtle bugs caused by shared mutable state.

Next, the piece maps encapsulation patterns to modern architecture: how microservice boundaries echo class boundaries, and why preserving encapsulation across service APIs reduces coupling and enables independent evolution. We discuss the Facade pattern as a way to present a simplified interface for complex subsystems and the Adapter pattern for integrating legacy modules without exposing their internals.

A substantial section covers common anti-patterns: exposing mutable collections, wide-use of public setters, and breaking encapsulation by leaking implementation details through API contracts. Each anti-pattern is followed by a step-by-step refactor showing how to restore invariants and reduce the cognitive load on consumers. The article closes with testing guidance: how to write unit tests that validate behavior rather than internal state, and how to use property-based and contract tests to assert invariants across module boundaries.

Examples, diagrams, and pragmatic rules of thumb are included so readers can apply encapsulation effectively in day-to-day development. The goal is not to hide all details, but to reveal the right ones — the intent — while keeping volatile implementation details private.

blogs.title: Inheritance vs Composition: Choosing the Right Relationship
blogs.author: Sarfaraj Khatri
blogs.description:
Inheritance and composition are fundamental tools for modeling relationships between types. Both are essential, but they answer different design questions. Inheritance models an  'is-a' relationship and enables reuse of implementation through a shared base type, while composition models "has-a" or "uses-a" relationships, favoring delegation over sharing code across a class hierarchy.

This article provides a practical, example-driven approach to choosing between inheritance and composition. We start with the fragile base class problem: how extending a base class can create subtle coupling and unexpected behavior, especially when the base class evolves. Concrete C# examples show how overriding behavior can break Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) assumptions and introduce runtime surprises.

We then move to composition: how small, focused strategy objects and clearly defined interfaces enable flexible behavior swapping and make systems easier to test. A worked refactor converts a deep inheritance hierarchy into a set of composable behaviors, demonstrating how composition improves discoverability and reduces the blast radius of changes. Performance considerations are discussed; in many modern runtimes the overhead of composition is negligible and outweighed by the architectural benefits.

The article also identifies when inheritance remains the right choice: when concrete types share a stable, semantically coherent contract and polymorphism across an "is-a" relationship is required. We provide a decision checklist and anti-patterns to watch for (e.g., inheritance used merely for code reuse rather than modeling a true relationship).

Finally, the article offers a set of refactoring recipes, tests to establish behavioral baselines before changes, and metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the migration. The emphasis is on pragmatic maintainability: changes should improve clarity, testability, and the ability to extend systems with confidence.

blogs.title: Polymorphism: Design for Extensibility
blogs.author: Sarfaraj Khatri
blogs.description:
Polymorphism enables code to operate on abstractions rather than concrete implementations. This principle unlocks extensibility: new behaviors can be added without modifying existing clients if the system depends on stable abstractions. In this long-form article we explore static (compile-time) and dynamic (runtime) polymorphism and practical patterns that use polymorphism to make systems resilient to change.

The article begins with language-level examples: interfaces and virtual methods in C#, type unions and structural typing in TypeScript, and how these constructs let disparate types present the same surface area to consumers. We illustrate how factories and dependency injection frameworks tie into polymorphism to decouple construction from usage.

Next, we present design patterns that rely on polymorphism: Strategy for selecting algorithms at runtime, Visitor for separating algorithms from object structures, and Template Method for defining skeleton workflows with overridable steps. For each pattern, we include code samples, test strategies, and trade-offs.

A significant portion addresses pitfalls: over-abstraction that hides business intent, excessively deep type hierarchies that hamper comprehension, and runtime performance considerations. We provide heuristics for when to introduce polymorphism and when a simple value-object or function may be a better fit.

The article wraps with practical guidance for API designers: favor small, meaningful interfaces; document invariants clearly; and provide extension points that are intentionally stable. With polymorphism used judiciously, teams can add features with minimal code churn and confidence that existing behavior remains intact.

blogs.title: Abstraction: Modeling the Problem Domain
blogs.author: Sarfaraj Khatri
blogs.description:
Abstraction is the practice of capturing the essential characteristics of a problem while hiding irrelevant details. Correct abstraction reduces cognitive load and enables reasoning about a system at a higher level. This article demonstrates techniques to discover and validate useful abstractions in software systems, with practical examples and anti-patterns to avoid.

We start by describing domain-driven approaches: how ubiquitous language helps teams converge on meaningful concepts, and how to translate those concepts into domain models — entities, value objects, services, and repositories. The article shows how to choose the right representation for data and behavior and when to introduce interfaces or DTOs to separate concerns.

A large section covers anti-patterns: premature abstraction, abstraction leakage (when hidden details surface unexpectedly), and overloading objects with responsibilities. For each anti-pattern, a concrete refactor shows how to simplify the model and move complexity to appropriate well-encapsulated modules.

We also discuss practical verification strategies: property tests, contract tests between services, and living documentation that keeps abstractions aligned with the domain. The article concludes with a checklist for evaluating abstractions: clarity (does the name match intent?), minimality (no extra responsibilities), and stability (likely to remain unchanged).

blogs.title: SOLID Principles: Building Maintainable Object-Oriented Systems
blogs.author: Sarfaraj Khatri
blogs.description:
SOLID is an acronym representing five design principles intended to make object-oriented systems more maintainable and extensible: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion. This article goes beyond definitions and shows practical application and trade-offs when applying SOLID to real projects.

For each principle we provide a deep, example-driven walkthrough. SRP (Single Responsibility) is reframed as focusing on reasons to change; the article shows how splitting responsibilities reduces mutation scope and simplifies testing. OCP (Open/Closed) is demonstrated using extensible plugin-like architectures and composition-based extension points. LSP (Liskov Substitution) is illustrated with concrete counter-examples where subclassing breaks client code, and refactors that restore substitutability.

Interface Segregation is discussed in the context of API design — why large, catch-all interfaces harm consumers, and how small, purpose-specific interfaces improve clarity and enable multiple implementations. Dependency Inversion is explained with DI containers, constructor injection patterns, and how depending on abstractions (interfaces) rather than concrete classes improves testability and modularity.

The article also addresses pragmatic concerns: SOLID is not a checklist to be applied blindly. We discuss situations where strict adherence may add unnecessary indirection and how to balance principles with simplicity. Each section contains C# and TypeScript code examples, testable refactors, and guidelines for code reviews that focus on maintainability metrics. The goal is to provide readers with a practical mindset for applying SOLID in day-to-day engineering work.
